problem:
Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. Trees are written in level order with null for missing children.

Example: root = [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] -> 3
Example: root = [1, null, 2] -> 2

data.key_insight: The maximum depth of a binary tree is 1 plus the maximum of the depths of its left and right subtrees. If a node is null, its depth is 0.

steps.title: Check Base Case
steps.detail: If the current node is None, return a depth of 0.

steps.title: Recursively Calculate Subtree Depths
steps.detail: Find the maximum depth of the left subtree and the maximum depth of the right subtree by making recursive calls.

steps.title: Combine Results
steps.detail: Return 1 plus the greater of the left and right subtree depths.

data.pattern_summary: Process a tree by breaking it down into identical subproblems for the left and right children, combining results as you return from the base cases.

pattern_options.name: Recursive Depth-First Search
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. The problem naturally breaks down into finding the depth of the left subtree and the right subtree.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers are used for linear structures like arrays or strings, not hierarchical tree structures.

pattern_options.name: Greedy approach
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. You cannot make a locally optimal choice at each step without exploring both subtrees to see which is actually deeper.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. We are computing a numeric property of a hierarchical structure, not searching for stored key-value pairs.

signals.phrase: Given the root of a binary tree
signals.hint: Points to a hierarchical structure that is naturally traversed using recursion.

signals.phrase: longest path from the root down to a leaf
signals.hint: Indicates that you need to check all paths to find the maximum.

data.brute_force_idea: Check if the root exists, then recursively compute the maximum depth of the left child and right child, returning 1 plus the larger of the two.
data.brute_force_why: Every node in the tree is visited exactly once.
data.bottleneck: The direct recursive approach is already optimal because every node must be visited at least once to determine if it is part of the longest path, resulting in O(n) time complexity.
bottleneck_hints: Consider whether you can solve this problem without looking at every node.
Think about what happens if you skip even a single node in the tree.
Since every node must be inspected, any valid algorithm must touch all n nodes at least once.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The recursive DFS visits every single node in the tree exactly once. By breaking the problem into independent left and right subproblems, we avoid redundant calculations and process the entire structure in linear time.

derivation.note: The base case check runs once for every node plus once for every null child.
Returns zero for each null child pointer.
Recursively computes the depth of the left subtree for every node.
Recursively computes the depth of the right subtree for every node.
Performs a constant time addition and max comparison for every node.

data.time_summary: Summing the execution costs across all lines gives O(n) total operations, which matches the measured wall-clock growth of n^1.06.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(h) where h is the height of the tree, determined by the maximum number of activation frames on the call stack during the deepest recursive descent.
data.takeaway: When dealing with tree structures where the result at a node depends entirely on its subtrees, use post-order recursive DFS to compute sub-results bottom-up.
mistakes: Forgetting to handle the base case where the root is null, leading to AttributeError.
Confusing tree height with tree depth and mixing up recursive return values.
Recomputing maxDepth redundantly instead of storing results in local variables like left_depth and right_depth.

events.label: Tutor: build the visual explanation

data.overview: The maximum depth of a binary tree is found by recursively computing the depth of the left and right subtrees and taking the maximum plus one. This divides the tree into smaller subproblems until reaching the base case of a null node.
data.intuition: Imagine standing at the root and asking both your children how tall their buildings are. You take the taller building, add one for yourself, and tell that total to the person below you.
